utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in the courtroom and also to those just outside the courtroom assisting us. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Are there any further reports on communications that may have taken place yesterday, in the afternoon, between Mr. Stewart and Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I've got -- may -- I've got two or three small points to report. May I just report them all, Your Honour, including that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The first is that Mr. Tieger and I met yesterday afternoon with Ms. Cmeric, actually. Ms. Cmeric and Mr. Tieger had had a long and animated conversation before we met. Their state of play is that Mr. Tieger is now very helpfully reducing what we agreed to writing. We're hoping to have an exchange of e-mails and produce some sort of note or memo or copy e-mail for the Trial Chamber which sets out what we've agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber would like to receive that as soon as possible because, you'll understand, your ongoing discussions are relevant for the Chamber's decision, so therefore we feel more or less obligated to wait until we have that result.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, we understand that. The very last remark that Your Honour has made really has to go in that direction across the court, because the ball is right now in Mr. Tieger's court. But we have the point, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to report to the court. Just before I came down, I saw Mr. Tieger and he has sent the e-mail, but I don't know that Mr. Stewart has had a chance to see it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Cmeric is probably reading it even as we speak, Your Honour. We'll catch up with it. I had left before it arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If Ms. Cmeric can continue to work as long as we speak, you might have quite some time to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The second point to report is this, Your Honour: I have to say that Mr. Krajisnik has just signed the agreement in relation to data transmission, so as soon as that's got to the powers that be in this particular instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm happy that the matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- it shall be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm happy that the matter has been resolved. As you may know, and as Mr. Krajisnik may also know, the Chamber has really tried to promote the availability of laptop and a use of that laptop that assists Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're very grateful for that, Your Honour. In fact, there was just all sorts of confusion about the agreement. It confused Mr. Petrov, me, Mr. Krajisnik, everybody. We got it sorted out. We put our brains together and eventually managed to work it out. It's done. There's no problem with that. A tiny point, Your Honour. Your Honour and I agreed yesterday afternoon that this extra allocation for interpreters was a $1.000. It's actually a thousand euro. Just to correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said dollars, because usually remuneration goes in dollars in this Tribunal, but I'm glad to hear that it's therefore 30 per cent more than I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Though I still feel the internal pain of Your Honours comment that people get paid in dollars, but that's another matter. So it's that, Your Honour. I just wanted to add to that, though, that if any such matters are at any time to be regarded by the Trial Chamber's relevant to anything to the adjournment application, then we would ask for an opportunity to deal with it, because to take isolated aspects of the financial arrangements without any regard to the whole can lead, with respect, to error and even to unfairness. So I know Your Honour is no more enthusiastic than we are, I believe, to explore that in these hearings, but as long as it's all left on one side, Your Honour, the Defence is content. But isolated aspects on their own really have to be disregarded, unless the whole matter is explored.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I just explain why I knew about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did not, and this Chamber would not, inquire into backgrounds of your submissions without letting the parties know. At the same time, when we were informed that this -- that Ms. Cmeric would leave the team, it was of some concern to the Chamber how communication with Mr. Krajisnik would take place, and whether any additional measures had been taken, just in view of the language problem. And this was not in relation to the adjournment, of course I know the departure of Ms. Cmeric plays a role in it, in the adjournment matter, because it causes additional problems. But it was not on the basis of your motion that we inquired into it, but it was mainly to our concern for the practical implications of the departure of Ms. Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, we understand that entirely, and we don't have any problem that Your Honours have that single piece of information, provided with the proviso that I've indicated. Your Honour will actually appreciate that it buys 40 hours of interpreters' time, which would get exhausted in eight days in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you would have a full-time assistant in court, that would not -- certainly would not help you out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. In fact, we did -- Ms. Loukas and I discussed it, we took the view that Ms. Hanson, the witness, giving her witness in English, where we felt there was relatively little B/C/S that would imply that that was not a priority for that resource given that we have B/C/S speaking witnesses coming up. So that is the explanation of the slightly unfortunate position that we are bereft of B/C/S facilities immediately. The last point, Your Honour, and I expect Mr. Hannis has something similar, although I did mention her yesterday, I should have introduced, my apologies, Ms. Vine to the Trial Chamber. I should have introduced my colleague, and I say my colleague because she is an English barrister, Ms. Catriona Vine, who is with us for the moment, not unhappily for very much longer. We'd like her to stay forever. She is here for the moment assisting us out of the goodness of her heart, If I could put it that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine. What could this Chamber add if Mr. Stewart says he'd like you to be on board forever. Welcome to this courtroom. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I also have an introduction to make before we start. Assisting me today in court is one of our trial attorneys, Anna Richterova. She joins the team. She previously worked on the Brdjanin case with Joanna Korner. As you know, Mr. Tim Resch and Magda Karagiannakis were part of our trial team but they have both left the Tribunal. However, we're hoping that Ms. Richterova can carry the load of both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Although Mr. Hannis didn't say he wanted to keep you forever, Ms. Richterova, I take it, is as happy with your presence as the Chamber is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: She is getting paid, but she's also here out of the goodness of her heart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No comment. Are you ready to continue the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, your Honour. And while we're having the witness in, I thought we could hand up binder number 3 because I only have two or three documents left in binder number 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Usher, could you please escort Ms. Hanson into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you, before you further give your testimony, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My case manager just stepped out to hand some copies of intercept translations to the booth, and when she returns, I'd like to hand the presentation binder to Ms. Hanson. When we left off yesterday, Your Honour, I think we were at tab 79 in the presentation binder, which is master tab number 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, we were still talking about the War Commission, and we had just gone through a series of documents regarding the appointments of commissioners. I believe this document has some reference to the abolishment of Crisis Staffs and the creation of War Commissions. Could you tell the Court about this one?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This document we had seen also yesterday in a slightly different context. This is a letter from the secretary of the executive committee of the SDS to the presidents of the Crisis Staffs of Serbian Autonomous Regions. In the first paragraph, he is telling them that Crisis Staffs have been abolished by the Presidency decision of 31 May, and instead of "Crisis Staffs," he says in this text, "War Commissions." As we know, the decisions specified War Presidencies. In the very next paragraph, he says War Presidencies. He tells these people that they should set up War Presidencies in the municipalities. I take this to be a confusion of terms. We saw it yesterday in our own translation, because it's -- as we saw the original decision says presidencies, not commissions, but he himself makes this error. As I indicate in my report, in many cases we see confusion of the terms, and this even among people who should know what the decision actually said. So it's an indication of the implementation of the Presidency decision on War Presidencies, indication that the -- these people who were, until now, presidents of the governments of these autonomous regions and presidents of their regional Crisis Staffs are now war commissioners. It's now significant that this is from the SDS to these governmental figures, and saying now, any questions or -- about the implementation, contact the Presidency directly, showing the contacts between the SDS and the Presidency, the overlap of party functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I don't recall if yesterday, when we first looked at this document, did you tell us anything about the parties to whom this document was sent?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't then. As I said now, each of these people, Bozidar Vucurevic, was president of the government of SAO Herzegovina. He was also, I believe, a member of the Main Board of the SDS. Milan Kostanic, we met in an earlier context -- no, it's the other Stanic. Excuse me. This is head of the SDS in Vlasenica. And Milan Novakovic, also a member of the Main Board and president of the SDS, but to my shame, I can't remember right now which municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, let me take you to the next tab, tab number 80. You also told us that there appeared to be some confusion about the transition from Crisis Staffs to War Presidencies, and then before that there was even time to even deal with that, it was decided to form war commissions. Did you see that reflected in some of the documents in the local municipality documents?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, that's how I drew my conclusions, is observing the confusion at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you go on, let me describe what this next document is. Presentation tab 80, master tab number 126.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say confusion, I mean simply that the evidence I have seen indicates that people do not consider that there was a significant difference between them, and that the terminology was not consistently applied because they did not consider there to be a significant difference. This document is a speech, judging from internal evidence given, or at least drafted, for the third anniversary of the founding of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac. As just a speech, one has to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, the document title says "Formal Speech on the Occasion of Declaration of the Rajlovac Municipality," and not "a third anniversary", and it bears as the date, 23rd February, 1992, which might be -- that would suggest that it would have been for the third anniversary that the Rajlovac Serbian municipality would have been established in February 1989, which is at least a bit of a puzzle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We believe the February '92 date is the date of the establishment, and there is internal information that leads us to believe that this was an event that occurred in February of 1995, so it's a retrospective. Your Honour, for the information of the Court and Mr. Krajisnik, the portion that we intend to highlight here, I think, is at page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'd suggest it might be a good idea -- I'm sorry, I think Your Honour has the same point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to have this clarified by the expert, because at least the text which I have not read, of course, starts with, "Today, on the 23rd of February, 1992," which does not seem to be in -- looking in retrospect to that date, but rather to address the -- so could you please clarify that with the expert. You have heard, Ms. Hanson, what the issue was, so if you would come up with a spontaneous explanation for us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've dealt with this issue myself, Your Honour, in trying to understand this document. If we could look at the original in Sanction, on the first page - maybe it's not immediately available in Sanction, the first page of that document - but you can see that it -- originally it said, "On this day in 1992," and that was crossed out and said "23 February 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We met ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what does that mean, "today".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this date, I would take it to mean, on this date in 1992, we met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "On this date", so "today" should be on the date of the 23rd of February. On the word of the text, the word is "dan," which is day, but -- Could we have it on our screen so that the interpreters can see it as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I comment, because I can't help on B/C/S but I can help on English. As far as the first line is concerned, it seems, from what the witness is saying, is there would be a very tiny solecism in the translation because "we have met" wouldn't be the English in those circumstances, it would be "we met," and "we have met" adds to the confusion, because it certainly suggests that it just happened, as opposed to three years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ask perhaps the interpreters if they could have page 1 of the computer evidence on their screen, I take it that what is stricken out -- I don't have the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, we could ask Ms. Hanson to read the three words in B/C/S that are stricken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the two lines on the top which are stricken are the reserves and respective guests. And then we have the original text. Could you please read that, what is stricken out, the three words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Na donis ne don [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the interpreters tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It means "today".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It means today.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: On this day or today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So do I understand that it is possible to understand this also on that day of -- on that day in 1992, not necessarily that being the present day in which -- on which the words are pronounced?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It means today, on this day, this particular day. Now, what that day was, perhaps the 23rd of February, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we see -- could you read what is handwritten, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 23rd of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that the interpreters have it now on their screen as well. That if you take out "today," could it mean on the 23rd of February, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then the translation is not correct to the extent that "today" has been stricken out. Yes. That's at least for the time being a clarification on the first three words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I would ask Ms. Hanson to clarify that if some of the further internal content reflects that this was clearly written after February 23rd, because there's a reference to April 21st, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely. It was internal -- it was other internal evidence. The very next sentence begins -- after that, the first sentence that was problematic says [B/C/S spoken], "that was the time" when -- or at that time many thought it was impossible. It's clearly, in hindsight -- they use the past tense referring to the day on which they formed the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are a hundred per cent endorsed. Your Honour was ahead of us. We were 100 per cent endorsing with respect, Your Honour's suggestion that the witness should give the clarification. But it seems that, overall, some improved translation of this document would be valuable. It's quite clear, for example, that it refers to three years of existence in an activity of the Serbian municipality of Rajlovac, which is a little bit of a clue. But what we have is we've got "dear sirs" appearing as if it's three draft letters, whereas, in fact, it appears to be a speech, so that "dear sirs" would be we suppose something like, well, say "ladies and gentlemen". Not sure how many ladies were present. But it's been translated in a way which, overall, seems to be adding to our confusion. So perhaps the whole document ought to be revisited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we could ask specific attention from the Prosecution. Is there any further dispute about this being a document - and I'm also looking to Mr. Krajisnik who, of course, can read the original - this document of a speech which looks back for three years?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may the interpreter add that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that appears to be so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters want to speak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- having read the document a little bit, it could be "on this day" in the sense, on the anniversary of this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It's clear. There's no dispute anymore. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, then, Your Honour. If I could direct you to the excerpts we wanted to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think in the English, at the bottom of page 3 in the third line of the second paragraph from the bottom and also at the top of page 4.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted first to show that the top of page 4, because the issue right now is the distinction -- whether -- how important was the distinction between War Presidencies and War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And for Mr. Krajisnik, I believe that would be the top of page 6, or 02269288 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The line there at the top of the English translation: "The War Presidency, then the War Committee," and in the English translation it should be "War Commission, has been the standard". And then again, "War Presidency were selected and their tasks were mostly the same." Other evidence I've seen indicates a similar inclination to see these bodies as much the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That was the point -- that was the immediate point we wanted to make with that document, Your Honour, was to show the continuing confusion about the distinction between War Commissions and War Presidencies and Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I wanted to move on now to another party report, Ms. Hanson, where you talked about the connection between the party and the Crisis Staffs with the military. And you, I think, have in the binders some examples of the roles of the Crisis Staff vis-a-vis the military.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report had followed -- there was another section in my report, but if we're going to the military, we can see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I guess I'm talking about, sort of, the nexus of the party and the government and the military --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because there's a different set of documents regarding military. Yes. The Crisis Staff, as we saw, was tasked to coordinate defence, so it coordinated with the military, also with the government and with the party. It was a coordinating body to make sure that -- make sure that all these different forces and resources in the municipality were working together and following the policies of the SDS. So the military was one important factor, but as a more complicated factor, then some of the others, I wanted first to just talk about in general how the Crisis Staff was a coordinating body.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And while we still have that Rajlovac document up, is there an example --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The very next sentence after the one I just read, second sentence on page 4 of the English translation, talking about the War Presidency, War Commission, said: "Each of these bodies concentrated to establish as close as possible cooperation with the military command in order to strengthen defence lines." And on the previous page, page 3 in the translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S, I believe it's on page 02269287.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: 85 -- 87, yes, yes. They describe in general how the Crisis Staff operated. It says: "In addition --" I'm sorry, Your Honour, this is the second to last paragraph on page 3 of the English translation. "In addition to the legally selected assembly and their organs, we have appointed a Crisis Staff that has been meeting in session on a daily basis and has been resolving current problems. The Crisis Staff participated in saving property, organising the Territorial Defence, taking over military facilities, and everything that, according to the Crisis Staff, was of interest to the Serbian people. Conclusions were being brought and the actions were fast." Your Honour, because I've used the original before, I had, for my own purposes, my translation was slightly different in terms of forms of verbs. No different in context. That's why I was stumbling. This shows, however, how the Crisis Staff worked, meeting daily, saving property, organising the TO, and taking care of everything that the Crisis Staff judged was in the interests of the Serbian people. That was, I thought, a good description of how Crisis Staffs worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to go back to, sort of, the initial premises regarding Crisis Staffs, part of their purpose was, to do that kind of work in the municipality during times of war or imminent threat of war when the municipal Assembly could not meet.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. The basic premise, as we saw in the instructions from 26 April 1992, and the later decisions and instructions, when the municipal Assembly could not meet, the Crisis Staff was to replace the municipal Assembly as the municipal authority, the highest authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And later on in your presentation, do you intend to give us some specific examples?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I want to present the Court with three case studies of municipalities to show how this was borne out in practice. I think looking through a series of Crisis Staff documents is a useful way to see how they operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a reflection of that role of the Crisis Staff, sort of, replacing the municipal Assembly during these times, I think, is in the next document at tab 81, master tab number 145?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the decision of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bratunac. It's numbered 01-I-92. It's not dated. That's why I give the number. But it shows what we'll see is typical for Crisis Staffs; that in item 2, "the organs of the Assembly and the executive committee of the municipality shall cease working and their competencies should be temporarily taken over by the Crisis Staff." And Article 5: "All decisions, orders, conclusions, and other documents in the area of the municipality shall be brought by the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bratunac," indicating the authorities which the Crisis Staffs claimed in the municipality on the basis of replacing the municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's the last tab in binder number 2. I want to move to presentation binder number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me try to get it. Mr. Hannis, perhaps you could pay attention to the fact that presentation tab 80, the title is different than what we find in footnote 46, because in footnote 46, the third anniversary appears where it does not appear on the title in tab 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll have a look at that. Now if we can hand presentation binder number 3 to Ms. Hanson, and if Your Honours could turn to the first tab in that binder, which is presentation tab 82, master tab number 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is another reflection of that role of the Crisis Staff in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the first page, which would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The bottom of the page, last paragraph?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I just didn't know if we -- on 02265800, and on the first page of the English translation, the last paragraph. This is an information from the executive board of Ilijas municipality, dated the 21st of December, 1992, and describes the course of the war in Ilijas. "At the beginning of July, in accordance with the legal acts of the Republika Srpska, the municipal Crisis Staff and the municipal wartime Presidency stopped their operations and started to work the municipal wartime commission executive board and municipal administrative organs. The municipal wartime commission is the link," or a link, "between the authority organs and the command of the Serbian army," again, showing the continuity between Crisis Staff and War Presidency and War Commission, and that the War Commission is a link between the municipal organs and the army command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Anything else from that document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's all I intended to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on to presentation tab 83, Your Honours, master tab number 141, from Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most, dated the 30th of May, 1992. If you note the makeup of the Crisis Staff, it is consistent with the instructions issued and, moreover, with the intention of the Crisis Staff as coordinating various political, military, and other forces. We see that the commander of the 6th Krajina Brigade is a member, number 10, Branko Basara; also number 6 and 7, the chief of the police station and the commander of the TO; number 4, the president of the Club of Deputies of the SDS in the municipal Assembly. And also of interest here is the description for number 2, Vlado Vrkes, the deputy president of the Crisis Staff, "in charge of political problems and the implementation of the ideas of the Serbian democratic party leadership at the level of the republic region and municipality." So we see this confluence of party, military, and government in one body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one additional question. We suddenly see here Nedeljko Radusa, which is a name not familiar to the Chamber. Could you please look at the original to see if it's a proper reflection of what the original says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is Radusa in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since this name has appeared before in this courtroom, it's good to know that the translation is not correct. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that document has already been presented to the Court in another exhibit, and we addressed that issue of the error in the translation at that time as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, in your report you talk about how Crisis Staffs operated as part of the overall Republika Srpska system, and how they not only viewed themselves, but how they were viewed from the highest level as being an integral part of that system. In tab 84, I think you have an example of that. This is master tab number 468, and this is from a national Assembly session in November 1994. Could you direct us to the quote that you wanted to highlight here?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the bottom of page 347 in the translation, and page 02153546 in the original. We looked at this passage before because it was a reference to the instruction A and instruction B. Karadzic reminds the deputies, "you remember about instruction A and B." He says: "We have Crisis Staffs and it was clear that they were the authority. They could make mistakes but they were the authority. The people were not left out the authority because there was a Crisis Staff." So I repeated it here just to highlight the fact that the Bosnian Serb leadership regarded the Crisis Staffs as their authority in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's move to tab 85 in the present --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I make an observation, please. I don't think it's a problem, but it's just that when Mr. Hannis introduced his question at page 18, line 22, I think it was, by saying "next you talk in your report as to how the Crisis Staffs operated," et cetera, et cetera, "viewed from the highest level as being an integral part of that system." I appreciate that all Mr. Hannis is trying to do is just identify the particular aspect of the witness' report which is being dealt with. We would just ask that, if possible, and if not too inconvenient, that when an introductory passage is included, that Mr. Hannis could give specifically the paragraphs in the report. I see him nodding. It seems that there's no particular problem about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's a point well taken, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That particular point was from paragraph 41 of her report. I should indicate, Your Honour, we now have copies of her report here, and we could have those handed around or marked as an exhibit at any time that's convenient for the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One more example regarding paragraph 41 of that point that you just mentioned, I believe at tab 85, this is an intercepted telephone conversation?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, between General Ratko Mladic and Fikret Abdic on the 21st of April, 1992. Just a very short passage that indicates, again, that the leadership saw Crisis Staffs as part of the state system.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is a long intercept but we're only going to play a short segment. In the English hard copy, it's at page 7. The third speaker from the bottom up is Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that the one, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the B/C/S for Mr. Krajisnik, I think that would be found on page 0322-0328, almost the middle of the page. And we'll try and play that now. I think it is very short.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Ratko MLADIC: Will you talk to them? Call the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and resolve the matter with them. Crisis Staffs and those associations are under their control."

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, Mladic says that at least he sees Crisis Staffs as being under the control of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this was a conversation from the 21st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In general, just to give us a little background of what that conversation was about between Mr. Abdic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was the withdrawal of the JNA forces, of what is being left behind and what is being taken with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I want to move to another topic regarding Crisis Staffs receiving orders from the higher levels of the government. Tab 86 is master tab number 165. And can you tell us what this is and what point you wanted to make by including this?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wanted to say that evidence which shows the way the Crisis Staffs were part of the state system is the fact that the leadership or state organs issued orders to crisis staffs, both to Crisis Staffs as a category in general and to individual Crisis Staffs. This decision is a decision of the Presidency, signed by Karadzic as president of the Presidency, dated the 2nd of June, 1992, the decision on the return of those who left the territory of the Serbian Republic of BiH -- I'm sorry, the return of those who left to the territory, I'm sorry. In both -- in Article 1, we see that people who left the Serb Republic are instructed to return and report to the Crisis Staff; if they can't go back to their place of residence, then the nearest Crisis Staff. In Article 3, it says: "The municipal Crisis Staff shall decide on the further engagement of those people who come back." Article 4 says: "Those people who do not explain or justify their inability to return to the Crisis Staff shall be denied the right of citizenship." And that those people will lose their -- their property will be used temporarily for the needs of the Serb republics, and the Crisis Staffs shall take care of and use that property. So the Presidency is clearly tasking municipal crisis staffs as a governmental category, with important tasks of deciding how to use the property of people who don't return, and deciding -- indeed, Article 4, deciding their right to citizenship, of people who don't return.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab number 87 in the presentation binder, master tab number 170.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order from the prime minister of the Serbian Republic, dated the 20th of May, 1992. I'm just looking at the -- although the preamble says the session held on the 21st of May. But it, similarly, is an order from the government tasking crisis staffs as a category. If you look at number 3, it says: "The order shall be sent to all municipal crisis staffs in the Serbian Republic. Municipal crisis staffs are required to transmit this order to the competent organs." So crisis staffs are seen as, again, a category to which the government gives taskings, and the transmission belt by which this order is passed further down to the municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And a point of translation. I see the name in the English translation is Branko Ceric.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the prime minister was Branko Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how is it spelled in the original B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Defence counsel is willing to agree that that should be Djeric, perhaps we can do that without having to have a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we wondered "how is it spelled in the original B/C/S" is going to come across on the transcript. But we do agree with that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any question, Your Honour, before I move on to the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that, in addition to these orders to all crisis staffs as a group, did you see examples of orders to specific crisis staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, and I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do have a -- Mr. Hannis, I do have a question. In the document which explains, as you said, the influence of the central government authorities of the crisis staffs, the document in tab 86, we see that in a document dated the 2nd of June, we find an instruction saying that "those who have temporarily left the territory of the Serbian Republic are obliged to return to their places of residence as soon as possible, until the 20th of May at the latest," which is a -- well, not easy to obey. Is there any interpretation or explanation of that? I see that, apart from that it's published in the Official Gazette of the 8th of June, that people -- you know, for criminal lawyers, retroactivity is a sensitive issue. Is there any explanation for that, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could offer one -- one possible explanation. I have not seen -- I have not seen a document that would explain it fully. But if you notice, the preamble says it's the acting presidents of the republic, but it is signed for Karadzic as president of the Presidency. And it may be that there was a decision earlier in May at the time that they had acting presidents, and when this decision was published in the Official Gazette, by then they had a Presidency and Karadzic was president of the Presidency. It may be that there was an earlier decision - I have not seen such a one - that was then published in the Gazette, without this discrepancy being --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and perhaps that would be a reference to an earlier decision than imposing an obligation on this at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And because some of these obligations here are continuing --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly an ongoing obligation. We will see that crisis staffs did act according to this decision later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the time period during which there were acting presidents within the republic, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I focussed on the municipal level and I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that was information that Mr. Treanor talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we go to tab 87. No, I think we talked about that already.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 87.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then to tab 88, which is master tab 180 -- 127. Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I connect that with tab 87. As you'll recall, 87 was the order from the president -- prime minister regarding mobilisation, and tasking Crisis Staffs to -- saying that they will get this order and act upon it. And tab 88 are the conclusions of the Crisis Staff of Sanski Most of the 21st of May, 1992, acting on a proclamation by the president of the Presidency, Karadzic, regarding mobilisation of forces and equipment. So it indicates that orders, such as mobilisation, were received and implemented at the municipal level. It's a linkage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have a question concerning tab 88. The Crisis Staff document from Sanski Most indicates that they're ordering this mobilisation on the basis of a proclamation from President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whether they got the decision directly from Karadzic or this -- as passed on by Djeric, because Djeric's order was, in turn, based on the decision of the president of the general mobilisation of forces and resources. It's not clear from this document how exactly the Crisis Staff received the order. But we know from Djeric's, that Crisis Staffs were sent that order from Djeric and we see it implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now I want to get to some examples of orders to specific Crisis Staffs. Tab 89 in the presentation binder, master tab 157. Please tell us what that is.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a letter from secretary of the government of the Serb Republic to the Crisis Staff of Ilijas, dated the 15th of May, 1992, asking them to arrange passage of a group of prisoners who are travelling from Pale to Visoko. So we see the government here coordinating between Crisis Staffs on the question of prisoner transport, and addressing a Crisis Staff individually.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And tab number 90 in the presentation binder, which would be master tab 158 in the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report on activities from the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo to the president of the Presidency. We'll look at it in a slightly different context again soon. But here it's noticeable that it is the Crisis Staff reporting to the president. And in this context, thinking of orders, I wanted to look at a later page --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Item number 8?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, item number 8, page 3 in the English translation, page 00855161 in the original, showing that they have received orders from the Presidency and granted them all the authority one would expect. The Crisis Staff -- this is the second sentence from the bottom. "The Crisis Staff has considered your draft decision made at the session on 5 June 1992 to form War Presidencies in Serbian municipalities, and has reached the conclusion," to summarise, "that there's no need for War Presidency here." On the next page, as they describe why they don't need a War Presidency, the middle of the next page, in the translation page 4: "We request that you consider the matter and give us urgent instructions and orders. It is our proposal that War Presidencies be established in municipalities under full occupation where it is impossible to operate in any other fashion." In this context, I want to show that this document shows that the Crisis Staff is receiving Presidency decisions, is reacting to them, and is requesting further orders and instructions from the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next in the presentation binder, tab 91.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I should like to go back a little bit to table 89, about the Ilijas Crisis Staff. I'm sorry for going back a little. In this document, in the last sentence, we read [In English] "... Ilijas municipality." I would like to ask the witness what this witness means, because my understanding is that these documents were seized, were found on site. The instruction was not in effect because the precaution was taken to recommend to destroy this document. Is this something that you came across in other documents or not, other documents with this type of recommendation. The last sentence is that we ask permission to be -- for this approval to be destroyed the moment the prisoners leave the territory of Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen any other such instruction on the document, but this document was found in the archives of the government, so it is perhaps a copy of a document that was sent to Ilijas Crisis Staff. It was not found in Ilijas, it was found in the government archives, which might explain why it wasn't destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this type of instruction was not found in other documents, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I have not seen anything with that phrasing. No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, I think we were just about to talk about tab 91, which is master tab 403.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the conclusions of the Sokolac Crisis Staff of the 20th of April, 1992. And here I bring your attention to number 4 on the first page of both the original and translation. "Competent organs should carry out the order issued by the Ministry of Defence of the Serbian Republic." And then says -- goes on to say that: "The president of the Crisis Staff and the commander of the TO staff will meet with the Minister of Defence on the account of the issue of keeping part of the equipment in the territory of Sokolac." I don't know -- we can't tell from this specifically which order, but nonetheless they've received an order from the Ministry of Defence, are instructing the municipal organs to carry it out, and want to meet with the minister to discuss it further. Again, of orders, implementation, and contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I just wanted to raise one point in connection with Judge Hanoteau's question before we talked about this. That order regarding the movement of prisoners in Pale, Your Honours, Judge Orie and Judge Canivell, will recall that we had a witness from Pale who testified live and we presented some documents in connection with the movement of prisoners from Pale at that time. And if it's of interest to the Judges, that's a place that I would direct you to have some reference that may have a link to that particular order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to move on to paragraph 41 in your report where you talk about Crisis Staffs operating as part of the Republica -- I'm sorry. Before -- strike that. I'm talking about what we just talked about. I want to talk about examples of Crisis Staffs, not necessarily receiving orders from the centre but receiving support from the higher level of the government. Did you find examples of that in your study?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found several examples that indicate that the government was materially supporting Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me direct you to tab 92 in the presentation binder, master tab number 173.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the minutes of the meeting of the government of the Serb Republic of the 18th of May, 1992. If you look at -- under item 1 in the minutes, the end of item 1, on page 2 in the translation, and that's 01245319 in the original, on the list -- numbered list, number 4, the Ministry of Finance was put in charge of giving aid, that is, 30 temporary loans, to Crisis Staffs, so the government is directing its Ministry of Finance to provide loans to Crisis Staffs. Then under agenda item 2 on the same page, bottom of the page: "It was concluded that aid be given to the Novo Sarajevo and Hadzici Crisis Staffs, and that the amount of aid be determined according to the situation in these municipalities."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at tab 93 in the presentation binder, master tab 174.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the next session, the 21st of May, minutes of the government session. Similarly, aid being discussed. Under agenda item 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you direct us to that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find it in the -- it's on page 3 in the translation, fourth item in the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the original?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the original ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The bottom of --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the ERN because it's just a highlighted section. 01245323, the bottom of that page. "Regarding the request of information for funds for the purchase of uniforms and of Crisis Staff, Stari Grad, Novo Sarajevo, Centre Sarajevo, Rajlovac, the finance minister to prepare a proposal." So, again, finance minister being tasked to see about funding some Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, presentation tab 94, master tab number 357. What does that show?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an overview of the budget of the Serbian municipality of Ilijas, from the 11th of May to the 30th of June, 1992. And in the first section on income, we see that the bulk of the income of the municipality, 13 million dinars out of 16.700.000 came from the Serbian Republic -- came from the government of the Serbian Republic. On the 11th of May, order number 18, 3 million; on the 22nd of May, order 60, 10 million. To give the Court some idea of roughly the order of magnitude at a time of inflation, 16 million, according to the official exchange rate, I looked at the official exchange rate for the 1st of June, to give a rough figure, it's the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 1st of June of --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of 1992, yes. Sorry. It's about $50.000, roughly, U.S. dollars. And the 13 million that they received from the government is about 40.000. It's about 80 per cent of their budget, anyway, came from the government. That's just to give you an idea of the order of magnitude.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's move to presentation tab 95, master tab 176.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a request for issuing of arms and ammunition, signed by the Minister of Economy. The exact addressee is not clear, but it's dated the 24th of May, 1992. And the minister is instructing that the Crisis Staff Grbavica, according to their request, be issued, as we see, machine-guns, automatic rifles, ammunition, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And quickly, tab 96, master tab 178.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: A request from the prime minister to the Bauxite Company, to the attention of Rajko Dukic, dated the 24th of May, 1992, asking the Bauxite Company to supply fuel for the needs of the Pale municipal Crisis Staff. So these show that the government gave monetary support but also arms and fuel to individual Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I do want to move on to another section of your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one question in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that in tab 95, it's the Ministry of Economy that provides the weaponry. I would expect some --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could also be industry. The word -- perhaps the interpreters can explain, but the word "[B/C/S spoken]" can mean both industry or economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could the interpreters help us out? But then, of course, you would have to read it. It says --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Ministarstvo Ekonomije."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ministry of the Economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But at least it's not the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it could also be "ekonomije" as industrial production.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That would, under those circumstances, mean that the ministry responsible for the production of weaponry would tell where the weaponry should be ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not know -- there is no addressee on this, so we don't know to whom -- to whom the Crisis Staff -- to whom this letter was addressed, who actually issued it to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Mr. Vitkovic was -- do you know that name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I wanted to move to paragraph 42 in your report where you talk about examples of the Crisis Staffs acknowledging the higher authorities on whose behalf they were acting or on whose orders they were following. Tab 97 in the presentation binder, master tab number 185.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the bulletin of the War Presidency of Kotor Varos, dated the 24th of July. It was simply a way in which the War Presidency described its work and informed the municipality. Under the section "Resettling the Population," page 6 in the translation, page 00416475 in the original, describing the moving out of Muslims and Croats, the third paragraph from the top of page 3: "The War Presidency and other relevant organs, showing full responsibility for these unfortunate people and acting in accordance with the existing laws and regulations of the Serbian Republic of BH, the region, and the municipality, has begun resettling the population in an organised fashion." I chose that passage because it shows that the Crisis Staff, or War Presidency in this case, took its actions, felt it was acting in accordance with the laws and regulations of the republic. We'll see this again in the case studies. In all kinds of decisions, large and small, they cite the law -- they cite laws and regulations and they see themselves as acting in accordance with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Another example of this is in presentation tab 98, master tab --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Prosecutor. Regarding this bulletin of the War Presidency, could you give us some clarification regarding the actual bulletins. Did they exist for all the War Presidencies? Did they exist for the Crisis Staffs? To whom they were addressed and how regularly they were addressed? Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not seen in every municipality such a bulletin. As we saw yesterday, we do have some municipal gazettes from municipalities, but this one is different, it's not an official gazette, it's of an informational newsletter. And I have only seen anything quite like this from Kotor Varos. I can't say that it didn't happen elsewhere, but this kind of informational newsletter as opposed to an official gazette, I've seen only here. I think we have about eight issues of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the Court's direction, I know from Sanski Most we did have a document called the "Informator", I think was the translation which was of a similar nature being more in the form of a narrative description. We also have a report on the work of the War Presidency in Brcko, which is more in the nature of a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question in relation to page 6 of tab 97. You showed that they acted in accordance with the existing laws and regulations of the Serbian Republic. What I'm interested in is whether I do understand the wording of this paragraph, on what was done in accordance with these laws and regulations. It starts by saying that many Muslims and Croats were feeling that they and their families were not safe, seeking a way out, and then later on it's explained that they had begun resettling the population in an organised fashion. Of course, resettling could mean a lot of things; to put them back in the place where they come from, but also to -- do I understand from what follows is that this activity is in accordance with the wishes expressed by these population groups and to the transportation and appropriate protection has been provided for such people as far as the first border area, that finally the activity was to escort them out of the territory? I'm also reading the next three lines: "Three convoys of such people have been safely escorted away to date." Does this mean that the activity, in accordance with the law, was to escort Muslims and Croats out of the territory, apparently at least that's what the document says, in accordance with their wishes as well and because they did not feel comfortable there? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to point, Your Honour, to the sentence on the convoys, but you saw it yourself. So yes, this document says that -- it's describing the process of organising convoys of Muslims and Croats and taking them out of the municipality to the first border area. This document says it was in accordance with their wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe we were going to look at -- I believe we were ready to look at presentation tab 98, master tab 187.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a proposal of the War Presidency of the Bosanska Krupa to the command of the 1st Podgrmac Brigade, dated the 25th of May, 1992. And the War Presidency proposes that the army prepare to cleanse the left bank of the River Una, including the right back of the Una, in the action; to -- and in the course of preparing and cleansing the left bank of the Una, to destroy and pull as many residential and other buildings as possible, including demolishing tunnels and setting fire to a forest. And what I found significant under "reasons," item 1 for this their reason for this proposal, is the political determination to have the border of -- the original is a little confused here, "to have the border of Serbian municipality autonomous region Banja Luka, Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a Serbian state established along the River Una up to Bosanska Otoka. The confusion of terminology, if you just read -- understand, the border -- everything borders here the municipality and the ARK and the state, so since those are our borders, the war -- as decided, Your Honours may recall that -- we'll get to it in the 12th May session of the Assembly, that was -- the borders were established there. So I see that -- I bring this here because the War Presidency is acting on the political decision and asking the army to take action on the basis of that political decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this is dated the 25th of May, about 13 days after the 12 May session, where the strategic objectives announcing the Una River as one of the borders were announced?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The Una River was specified as the border at the 12 May session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now we have a few minutes left before the break. Let me move to another topic that's related. In paragraph 43 of your report, you say, in addition to acknowledging the central authority of the higher bodies, the Crisis Staffs also reported to these higher organs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Reporting is an important indication of the -- both the communications between the municipal level and the republican level but also of the hierarchy. So the next tab, or should you say it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Tab number 99, master tab number 193.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the minutes of a session of the National Security Council and the government of the Serbian Republic of the 20th of April, 1992. And if you see number 9: "The reports on the works of Crisis Staffs and municipal governments were adopted." Number 10: "Suggestions on the use of the -- of previous reports by the Crisis Staffs were adopted." So the National Security Council and government has received reports on the work of Crisis Staffs as early as the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Earlier -- I just want to make reference to tab number 45, which we talked about yesterday, which was a telex from Bijeljina Crisis Staff. Do you recall that one --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from Bijeljina Crisis Staff dated the 1st of April, to the SDS Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that one of the earliest examples?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had examples of reporting via the Assembly throughout that period, but of -- that is -- Bijeljina, as we know, is one of the -- where the conflict broke out earliest, and it's a report on the day of the takeover of Bijeljina, the main -- the Crisis Staff is reporting to the Main Board of the SDS on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's move to tab number 100 in the presentation binder, master tab number 158.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document we saw earlier that I said I would be discussing in a slightly different context. I don't mean to fill up my binders, but I use one document for different purposes. And in this case, it is clearly a report on activities of the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo to the Presidency, dated the 5th of June. And I noted here, on page 3 in the translation, page 00845160, that one of the activities on which the Crisis Staff reported to the Presidency is the treatment of Muslims and Croats. It says: "Our public attitude is very correct. Secretly, the police apply the usual procedure to people who were engaged in military activities against us."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to whom was this report directed?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last page, page 5 in the translation, indicates that copies were sent to Radovan Karadzic and to Ostojic. Velibor Ostojic was the Minister of Information in the Serb Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you see some evidence that reflected that this report had, indeed, been received at a higher level? Let me take you to tab 101, master tab 191.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This report appears to have been received and discussed at the government level. This document is the minutes of the government session of the 7 of June, 1992. And we'll see on the agenda, agenda item 6, the report of the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. If we look further in the minutes -- I'm sorry, you'll see under the attendees, you'll see that Velibor Ostojic was there, and just under the minutes, under 6, the government acknowledged the report of the Crisis Staff -- the report of the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. So it appeared that that report was, in indeed, received and acknowledged by the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're one or two minutes early but would this be a good point to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I can ask a question to the witness first. I do understand that we're going, to some extent, which you mentioned in footnote 63 of your report. I don't know if you have your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we provide the witness with her report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 43, page 18, it says: "The 43, page 18, it says: "The Crisis Staff report to central state organs of the Republika Srpska, including the Presidency, the Assembly, and various ministries," and then reference is made to footnote 63. If I go through footnote 63, I have difficulties to find confirmation that the Crisis Staffs reported to the Assembly. Could you tell me where we find that in footnote 63?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Novo Sarajevo, it perhaps doesn't indicate actually putting that the intention that the Crisis Staff was formed by the Assembly of the Serbian People, that is, the Assembly should discuss the Crisis Staff's work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's different. You're right that they reported, not that it was their duty to report to the organ that had founded these Crisis Staffs. But you're right, the Crisis Staffs reported to the central state organs, and you give, then, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight examples of such reporting. And I have some difficulty in finding reports to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I showed with the Assembly sessions, which we will also see more in the next few documents in my presentation, are members of Crisis Staffs reporting to the Assembly on what happened in their municipality. It was not the Crisis Staff as an organ but members of Crisis Staffs informing the Assembly of what was going on in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you make a distinction between Crisis Staffs and members of Crisis Staffs. Do you also make a distinction between the Assembly and members of the Assembly? Because I see at least in footnote 63, and that was where I had some doubt, but of course I've not seen the document, the last item is Zivinice SDS Crisis Staff sent an appeal to Krajisnik. Of course, Mr. Krajisnik is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and, in fact, in that document, it specifies to Krajisnik -- to the president of the Assembly, it's sent to him as president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So he was addressed as --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As president of the Assembly. So it was not a report to the Assembly directly but to the president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, I do understand, that apart from this example, I do not find any examples of reports to the Assembly in footnote 63; is that correct?.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not reports as a written report. We'll see, as I say, an Assembly discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps not a footnote. We'll find other matters, but not in 63.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. We'll have a break until 11.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed -- Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I indicated to Mr. Hannis, just very briefly, I have two points to mention. I did say to Mr. Hannis -- they're very brief. One is positive, one is not so positive. The positive is that we're very close to agreement between Mr. Tieger and myself. I looked at the e-mail exchange, and subject to one or two observations, I'm fairly confident we'll sort that out in the next break. If that's over-optimistic, which I don't think it will be, we'll certainly do it very shortly after court and get something to Your Honours. We're, in principle, agreed. It's just a question of putting it in a suitable form for Your Honours, so it records one, two, three, four, five, six where we are. The second point is this: I've just been informed that I'm simply unable to give or leave with Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, let me stop you. I have been informed about the problem you have. It's a practical matter which need not be discussed in open court. It's about your ability to give the binders to Mr. Krajisnik so that he can consult them in the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours it has implications, it has implications for the very issues -- I'm not revealing in court anything improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no, it's just --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- I don't know anything about security details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm suggesting to you that we'll try to find a solution during the next break, and I'm available to assist you in that respect. But I already gave you some guidance that there is a relatively strict set of rules in respect of various parties, including the Dutch police force, who is responsible for the transportation from the -- this building to the Detention Unit. There are other services included, such as the OLAD and the Detention Unit. They have all their own responsibilities. I do agree that we should find the most efficient way of making it possible for Mr. Krajisnik to consult the documents, but I'd rather not discuss it in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- I am grateful for Your Honour's offer of assistance in this. The only comment I would make, Your Honour is this: It has inevitably -- it is a further drain on time and money for the Defence team to deal with this problem, and I hope that is understood. And in our submission, it is unfortunately a wasteful expenditure of further money and time in dealing with solving this particular difficulty. So if Your Honour can help us with that, it will improve the use of resources to that extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's see what we can do. Before I give you an opportunity to proceed, Mr. Hannis, Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to the witness, I take it in relation to one of the previous documents, or the present one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again, I'm asking you to go back a little. I hope nobody will mind. Tab 98, please. Madam Witness, I understand that you have drawn our attention to the fact that these War Presidencies or War Committees had true authority, according to my understanding, over the military commanders. I'm a bit surprised to find in this document the word "proposal," which, to my understanding, means a proposal, a suggestion. When you have hierarchial reports, then one might think it would be an instruction, a command, an order, to this commander of the 1st Brigade. Could you give me some clarification of this point? Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a very important question, the question of the command authority of Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies. As we'll see, I have a series of documents, quite an extensive part of my presentation is devoted to that issue, because there is no one simple answer. Some Crisis Staffs did order the military units in their municipalities; others saw their function as more limited to coordination and support. So we see a range of -- a range in the extent to which Crisis Staffs could or did command. So we'll see -- there will be orders, there will be recommendations, there will be -- simply providing the troops and the logistical support. In this case, the fact that it's a recommendation to a brigade suggests that this War Presidency is not claiming command authority over this brigade, if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. During the break, I spoke with one of the interpreters who suggested that it might be helpful with them that, because I think -- because the witness and I speak so rapidly sometimes, if, when she were reading from a document, if we can put the English up on the ELMO, we'll have the B/C/S up in Sanction, and that will assist them in following along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So that everyone can choose his language by pushing the buttons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I think, Ms. Hanson, if I can ask you, for example, in the next one, which is an excerpt from an Assembly session, if you could put the English, with the assistance of the usher, up on the ELMO and follow along in that for the interpreters, that would help. When --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For everyone in this courtroom, therefore, we would get the B/C/S on the button of "Computer Evidence," and to that extent the technicians are instructed to have the English text on the video selected for appearing on the screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now Ms. Hanson, I want to move -- one of the last questions we had before the break had to do with reporting from the Crisis Staff to the Assembly, and I think you indicated that you didn't have an example of -- a written report from a Crisis Staff directly to the Assembly, but you had examples of Assembly members who were also members of their local Crisis Staffs, giving oral reports.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We have a number selected in the next ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With that, let me go to tab 102 in the presentation binder, which is master tab 465, from the May 12th, 1992 Assembly session. Could you find the excerpt you want to talk about in connection with this tab and put the English on the ELMO for us. And then if you could tell us who is speaking.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at -- this section down here. Yes, on page 16, the speaker addressed here is Dr. Beli. Dr. Beli is Milenko Vujinovic, president of the Brcko SDS, member of the Main Board from Brcko and on the Brcko Crisis Staff. Here he is reporting on the situation in Brcko. Four lines from the bottom, he says: "For a definitive clearing of the area, it will be necessary to have many more forces." As I'm sure Your Honours has seen until now, the word [B/C/S spoken] is variously translated as cleaning, cleansing, clearing, but that is the word used here, [B/C/S spoken]. Later on in his speech, on the next page, page 17, I found it interesting, the middle of this paragraph, middle of the first paragraph, he notes that there are only 20 per cent Serbs in Brcko, and he's implying that it's been difficult to get them all mobilised. These Serbs are not getting easily involved in the conquests. And he notes that also in neighbouring municipalities, it's been difficult to mobilise men. There are a number of other speakers at this session. The next -- can I see the B/C/S just to know which section was next? It was Trifko Radic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
