utterances.text: I believe he speaks at the beginning -- bottom of page 18 and the top of page 19?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Starting at the top of page 19, the top of the page, up there, he describes -- Trifko Radic, excuse me, is a member of the Crisis Staff from Ilijas municipality and a deputy from Ilijas. He says that in Ilijas, they had been aware of the war, and they've been organising as well as they could, saying that "we have gotten arms" -- he says he will not speak of the arms, but he obviously is speaking of the arms. I'm sorry, it's confusing to move between the highlighted B/C/S and -- is it this one? He says in the next paragraph that -- actually, could I have this one. Sorry, just mastering the technology. In the next paragraph, he says that communications had been broken off, "so sometimes we don't know what to do. Should we --" this one - "should we defend -- should we destroy all the Ustashas and enemies around us or should we stop?" So he's asking the Assembly to set our goals and tasks, see what is ours, occupy it. And then next page -- I'm finding it difficult to work this way. At the bottom of page 19, he says that: "The Assembly tells us that our enemies must be given an exit route from Sarajevo" but he says that "they can pass through Ilijas only dead." And on the next page of the translation, page 20, in the top paragraph he describes their preparations, stealing goods and provisions, including oil, fuel. "We have cut off and mined the railway line and now no one can get into Sarajevo. We have mined the motorway too." So Radic is reporting to the Assembly on preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question. The comment you read about -- the quote was, I believe, "through Ilijas, they can pass only dead." What was that referring to? What was that discussion?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exit from Sarajevo, that he will not allow any Muslims to leave Sarajevo through Ilijas municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I can take you to one point further up in the preceding highlighted portion where you talked about the communication having been cut off and what should -- "we don't know what to do." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the bottom of the paragraph --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to talk about that a little later. It's highlighted but it's for another passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll address that at a later point.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, was there another speaker that we heard from before in the Assembly that you wanted to mention about here?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Miroslav Vjestica has a very extensive speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's at page 24 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would it be possible to have a different copy on the ELMO or are there not enough copies?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sure. We can give them mine if I can have it --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you'll need yours. Because it's a very long speech, it's hard to move around. This is Miroslav Vjestica, as we know, member of the Crisis Staff of Bosanska Krupa, telling the Assembly what they have done. In the middle of the -- I need to see both. In the middle of the page, he says: "What have we done in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa? I must tell you, to remind you all, that only 24 per cent of the population are Serbs in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. There are 14.500 of us and there are 47.000 Muslims." Later in that paragraph he says: "For a year and a half we have been preparing for war in Krupa." He says: "How did it happen that two-thirds of the town were taken in two days of operations? Thank god we did get to our borders, because that is how we had envisaged them and drawn them, and your peoples deputies know well that we said the right bank of the Una River would be our border, and the right bank of the Una River must be the border." He also talks about the military preparations and operations. "We have mined the right bank, we have mined the iron bridge, blown up the wooden one, and now we are preparing for Bosanska Otoka. God willing, in two to three days we shall mine the bridge in Bosanska Otoka." He says further down in the same paragraph: "There are no more Muslims in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All the enclaves that were there, we have evacuated them so that there will be none there for the duration of war operations. Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely, after our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border." On the next page, he also tells the Assembly about some other municipalities. On the third paragraph on page 25, he says that he's been in Bosanski Novi yesterday. "Bosanski Novi is sealed off, an ultimatum issued, and a deadline set for the Muslims to surrender their weapons." And he says: "The same is going on in Sanski Most. I think that the Muslims will soon be disarmed there too." In this context, I would like -- I had also been struck by Vjestica's comments at a later Assembly session on the 17th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think -- I think we have that in the next tab, 103 in the presentation binder, master tab 405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as not to cause any delay, I will stick to 102, and on page 19, the second paragraph, the tenth line I think, it's a paragraph that you read, madam. "Should we destroy all the Ustashas and enemies around us, or should we stop?" Do you see that? That's why I asked, as the president said, "Let us set our goals and tasks," what does the phrase "as the president said" imply as I haven't read the whole text and I would like to know what this refers to as the president said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just looking at the original to see what the term for Presidency -- I'm sorry, I'm trying to look for the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I see 7727 on the screen? It must be easier. Predsjednik, president, I just wanted to make sure that it wasn't perhaps the word for the "presiding" of the Assembly. He was referring, I assume, to an earlier speech by Karadzic at this Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I believe we were going to talk about an excerpt from the December 17th, 1992 session, presentation tab 103, master tab 405.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just in further reference to Vjestica, talking about the removal of Muslims from Krupa, you note that he says at the top of page 72 - this is in December 1992 - "Krupa is a newly formed municipality with 13.760 Serbs, and we prepared ourselves hard for one year before the war, when there were 47.000 Muslims there. We did our job."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me move to the next tab, which is presentation tab 104, master tab 392, and this is an excerpt from the July 1992 session, the 17th session.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had inserted that tab from the December session simply to reference Vjestica's remarks, but there were other remarks from the 12th of May session that I was still going to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have another one at tab 105 --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- from Mr. Radic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, sorry. So 104 is the -- if I could see on the screen which one that is. From Prstojevic. It's on 02149561, page 65 of the translation. This is from Nedeljko Prstojevic, who was president of the Crisis Staffs of Ilidza. He says: "When the Serbs started the uprising in Sarajevo, and when they seized control over certain territories, there was no government, or at least it was not known where it was then. Moreover, we even did not know if Mr. Karadzic was alive during the first couple of days. When we learned that he was alive, and when he visited us in Ilidza and encouraged us, the Serbs from Sarajevo retained control over the territory and even extended their territory in some areas, driving the Muslims out of the territories where they had actually been majority." So president of the Crisis Staff is reporting that they had driven Muslims out of territories where they had been a majority. Although he does mention a breakdown in communications, he says that it was only for a few days, and Karadzic then visited Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me return you to tab 105, master tab 465. Now back to the May 12th Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's slightly confusing. I am hopefully not troubling the Court. This is a speech by Trifko Radic, starting on page 48. As I said, Trifko Radic was -- we earlier saw him reporting on -- that they had stolen fuel, he said, and he's explaining in response to a question about that. He also describes the war operations. In the middle of the last paragraph, he says: "We are at war. We are surrounded. We are being attacked every evening. We have no other solution but to shell and destroy towns. We have destroyed one-third of Visoko. Maybe tonight another third will go." So he's describing to the Assembly the destruction of towns.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, I want to take you back to the July Assembly session, the 17th session, tab 106 in the presentation binder, master tab 392. And I believe you wanted to refer to --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The speech by Rajko Dukic, beginning on page 70 in the translation. It's a long speech so I'll be summarising. It might be hard to follow on the ELMO. But he's complaining at first that there are too many Muslims -- or the Muslims have too much authority in Bijeljina. This is the bottom half of page 71. He's saying -- he says that there's been some appointments of Muslims in Bijeljina. "I ask you then why we expelled all Muslim judges from Vlasenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik." In the context, he's thinking that was a good thing, "but it's pointless if we're letting Muslims run Bijeljina." On the next page, he goes on to talk about how much -- what will be the position of Muslims in Bijeljina, and then he sees, Birac, Birac being the area for which he was appointed coordinator. It is the municipalities of Bratunac, Vlasenica, Sekovici, parts of Srebrenica, Zvornik, that area. He says: "In Birac, Birac has 1.200 Muslims. That is how many there were, but I hope that has been at least halved, and 90.000 Serbs." So he's telling the Assembly that he hopes 60.000 Muslims no longer live in that area. At the bottom of that page 71, he requests that the Assembly issues an order that all Crisis Staffs and War Presidencies be closed down. "Wherever civilian authorities can function, they must function as tomorrow, and the military command must do its job." Just further indication of the authority of the Assembly's regard. He also says earlier in that speech, just noting that the municipality of Milic is functioning well. So it's more reporting of how the municipal authorities are doing and what they are doing in the Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I had just one fine translation point for you. I believe in my copy of the English page 70, where the beginning of that speech is, it lists the speaker as Rajko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you have a look at --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is added in hand, but it is a D, if you can put that on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The B/C/S page, 02149567?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's up on the ELMO now. It is a Cyrillic D and not an L. It was apparently an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from the content of the speech --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's consistent with Rajko Dukic, who, as I said, was appointed coordinator for SAO Birac, and he was chairman of the SDS executive board. And as far as I know, there was no Rajko Lukic, assemblyman.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The next tab in our presentation binder is 107, master binder number 2. I believe you indicated that this was simply for identification purposes, related to Mr. Dukic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the translation here also has both Lukic and Dukic, but that was simply to identify his appointment to Birac, to explain his knowledge of SAO Birac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the next topic I wanted to deal with, you talked of the role of Assembly deputies and transfer of their power to the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to explain the importance of the Assembly as both the channel upward for communicating the events on the municipalities to the republican level, and downward as the communicators of the Assembly authority to the municipal level. There's some discussion in the various Assembly sessions on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next tab in order is 108. Is that the one you want to talk about now?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I could see what the highlight -- if I could see the -- let's see --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Presentation tab 108, master tab 392.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Jovo Mijatovic. On page 58 of the translation, and page 02149554 in the original, in the middle of page 58, he says: "It is the MPs," that is, the members of parliament, "who are to transfer the authority of the Republic to the municipalities and from the municipalities here," an indication of their view of the role of assemblymen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Remind us again of who Jovo Mijatovic was?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an assemblyman from Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 109 is also from an Assembly session on the 17th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Once again, we have Milenko Vujinovic from Brcko, indicating the authority of the Assembly. He says: "Following the instructions of the Serb Assembly, a War Presidency has been formed in Brcko, and it replaces the local Assembly. We cannot invoke the Assembly. All the local representatives are in war. So instead of a War Presidency, we formed a military council." The original, I would note, is "Ratna Komisija," or War Commission. "We have followed your decision. You are forming a military council now that will consist of the mayor. Can you listen? Tell me what to do." So he is appealing to the Assembly saying that they have followed the instructions on forming a War Presidency and a War Commission, and looking for further instructions. Later on in this same session, I believe -- no --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I next had an excerpt from a different session, on the 24th of March, at tab 110 in the presentation binder.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we don't --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Master tab 389. Mr. Karadzic is speaking.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This one is a little out of order. I apologise for the confusion. It was meant to go a little more smoothly. This is from an earlier session. I do apologise for the confusion, it was meant to be of more -- On the 24th of March, 1992, Karadzic says: "The deputies are members of the supreme organ of authority, the Assembly. Now they must literally stay with the presidents of municipalities." Just emphasising there, we have seen this before, but to emphasise that he's saying that the deputies are the members of the supreme organ, and they go down and ensure that the policies are carried out by the presidents of municipalities. So this was a ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll get you back to the point I think you were heading before. Tab 111 in the presentation binder, master tab 405, from the December 17th session of the Assembly. And the speaker, again, is --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again, it's Milenko Vujinovic from Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, may I just interfere. In relation to tab 110, of course, it's the testimony of this witness that it's Mr. Karadzic speaking. But for the Chamber, it's rather difficult to go through the whole of the transcript at the same time while studying, so if you can include at least one page, giving a clue to who is the speaker at that time for the future, that would be highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On page 70 and 71 of the translation, Dr. Vujinovic says: "If I didn't follow the directives of this Assembly and the SDS, then for seven months I have been working wrong." I take that to mean, I have been following your directives, the directives of the Assembly and the SDS, so tell me what to do. As we know, he earlier said in the Assembly session, Tell me what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Milenko Vujinovic from --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Brcko, a member of the SDS main board and president of the Brcko SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And he's also referred to sometimes as?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Beli.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I want to move on to another topic which relates more specifically to the accused in this case, Mr. Krajisnik, and his contact with war commissioners or Crisis Staffs. Did you find some evidence in regard to that issue in preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found evidence of direct contact between Mr. Krajisnik and Crisis Staffs and also War Commissions and war commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's begin with presentation tab 112, master tab 195.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an announcement -- this is a document from Radio Ilijas, dated the 29th of June, 1992. We have other such texts. They all appear to be the text read by the broadcaster. It's a radio text. It notes that, in the fourth paragraph of the translation: "A delegation of the Presidency of the Serbian BH and the Main Staff of the Serbian BH army came to Ilijas, headed by Momcilo Krajisnik, president of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic." In the next paragraph, it notes that Ratko Adzic and Momcilo Krajisnik spoke, Krajisnik on behalf of republic organs, the Serbian Bosnia or west Serb, as Krajisnik said. "Then after the ceremony, the delegation visited the municipal Crisis Staff for a short period. There they were informed about the situation on the field and those Serbian units holding the --" and that the Serbian units held their positions. So Mr. Krajisnik visited a Crisis Staff as a member of the Presidency, and was briefed on the situation in the field, according to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Your Honours, I have a few intercepts we want to try and play. Tab number 113, and we'll try to put the English on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't need the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is master tab 406, reportedly a conversation between Jovan Tintor and Momcilo Krajisnik. And we're bring this excerpt about the middle of the page, in both the English and B/C/S translation -- transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Jovan Tintor: I'm calling from the headquarters. I hear you've been informed. Rajko has told me about that part. They're getting ready up there. Reportedly, they're on the move already. Momcilo Krajisnik: Who's on the move? Jovan Tintor: Well, the Muslims from Kobilja Glava. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah? Jovan Tintor: They're on their way towards Graoviste, towards us, Zuc, and the situation is tense. I think a conflict will break out up there. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah? Jovan Tintor: Please, it's my duty to inform you what's going on. Are you finished with -- I can't think of anything else but to check on some supplements to the military. Momcilo Krajisnik: You're calling from our SDS? Jovan Tintor: I'm calling from the Vogosca headquarters. Momcilo Krajisnik: Vogosca. Jovan Tintor. Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: Look, I've just spoken with Rajko. Jovan Tintor: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: I told him to inform this Momo Mandic for the police, you know. Jovan Tintor: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: Best man, we need to try everything to calm the situation down. Jovan Tintor: Yes. Momo Mandic has been on the spot. Momcilo Krajisnik: That's the most important thing. Finally, the people do need to organise themselves, but in no circumstances should be look for trouble. It is very important to keep peace, you know. Jovan Tintor: Yes, but they are on the move, best man. Momcilo Krajisnik: I don't think they are. Jovan Tintor: Well, let's hope so. If they're not, then it's -- Momcilo Krajisnik: Look, could you check this somehow? Jovan Tintor: Well, I have just received the information on the movement. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yeah, because there's panic. You check this. All right. There may be something going on, but you need to check on this panic. Jovan Tintor: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: Check it and let me know. I'll be here."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us who Jovan Tintor is?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of the Vogosca Crisis Staff. I'd also just like to note that when Tintor says, "I'm calling from the Vogosca headquarters." The word in the original is [B/C/S spoken], which means "headquarters" but also "staff". So the head of the Vogosca Crisis Staff is calling Momcilo Krajisnik, saying it's my duty to inform you. Krajisnik is being informed of the situation on the ground, we'll be talking to Momcilo Mandic about it. Momcilo Mandic was at this time, I believe, deputy minister of the interior, and so it shows his contacts with the head of the one Crisis Staff and his information -- his involvement following events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to next go to presentation tab 114, master tab 407.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the excerpt we're playing in English begins on page 2 of the English, Your Honours, and the third line on page 2 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo Krajisnik: Are you all right? What is it? Tell me, what's the situation like? Momo Garic: Well, there are some little problems. Could you receive me up there for a brief meeting? Momcilo Krajisnik: Well, sure, no problem. Momo Garic: You could, right? Momcilo Krajisnik: Sure. Momo Garic: Alright, I'll come there. I'll find some vehicle and I'll come there. Momcilo Krajisnik: Alright, Momo. What's the situation like up there? Momo Garic: Well, it's all right for the time being. We've had some casualties and many wounded. Momcilo Krajisnik: You did? Well, are our men withdrawing from up there? Momo Garic: No, no, but the cooperation here is not on a high level. I don't know why. Momcilo Krajisnik: Alright. Momo, come here, let's not discuss this over the phone. Momo Garic: Alright."

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momo Garic, as we saw from an earlier document, I think it's the next tab, simply for ID purposes, was a member of the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staff. And once again, we have him calling Krajisnik to discuss problems on the ground. Krajisnik saying sure, come up, have a meeting, clearly available to Crisis Staff members, and interested in the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, in these two last cases, the speakers addressed each other in what capacity? What was the capacity of Mr. Krajisnik for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not explicated in the phone conversation in what capacity they called, whether as president of the Assembly or a leader of the SDS or -- it's not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it's not clear, may I draw your attention to tab 113, where, not in the part read out by you but one of the first lines, it reads: "Could I speak with the speaker?" Is that, you say, there's no indication whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is how Tintor refers to Krajisnik as the speaker, meaning the speaker of the Assembly. But that he called him -- he also calls him "best man" later on. So why he called Krajisnik in that -- he may refer to Krajisnik as the speaker because he was the speaker of the Assembly, but why precisely he's -- in what capacity he's calling Krajisnik, that is one possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean that even calling him by one of his functions, that that does not necessarily imply that you approach him --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he's calling his office -- he's apparently calling Krajisnik's office, so he's asking the secretary, "Can I talk to the speaker?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That could also mean, for a friendly talk, you could also ask the secretary, if you want to speak to a friend, to ask the secretary to be connected with the speaker.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe you indicated tab 115 was just a document we'd seen before to show that Garic was a member of the Crisis Staff of Novo Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's why it's included.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, tab 116 is an Assembly that session we don't intend to use, so we're going to withdraw 116 and not use it for the purposes of this presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like to skip, then, to tab 117 in the presentation binder, which comes from the May 12th Assembly session. And again, I believe, starting at page 18 in the English, we have Mr. Radic, Trifko Radic, speaking again.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was Radic's speech. That was what I wanted up there. Where did it have it? It was a highlighted portion that I hadn't talked about. The middle of page 19, the last sentences of the middle paragraph, Radic says that "at the intervention of the president of the Assembly, we released that Ustasha, that Ivo Stanic, whom I had taken prisoner. This is what I regret having done most." I note it here because it's indicating that Radic received a direct intervention -- I'm sorry, received an intervention from the president -- from Krajisnik as president of the Assembly, and released a prisoner upon his intervention, even though Radic did not want to do it. So another indication of contact from Krajisnik to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have any further knowledge or information about who that particular individual was or what was that about?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't research that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, Your Honours, I want to move to tab 118, which are the minutes of the 15th session of the Presidency on the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have seen this before, but just to remind, in context of this discussion, that Krajisnik had been appointed as member of the Presidency responsible for the work for -- responsible for commissioners. I also found evidence of his involvement in the work of commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in connection with that, we'll have some more intercepted conversations, Your Honour. Tab 119, master tab 408. The excerpt we'll play begins on page 2 of the English, near the middle of the page. And in the B/C/S, it's about six blocks up from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you have that, Ms. Hanson?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's on the ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo Krajisnik: OK, tell me how things are going in Rajlovac. You know ... Mirko Krajisnik: Which things? Momcilo Krajisnik: That man from the municipality? The one that came recently, the commissioner?. Mirko Krajisnik: Yes, yes. He is not there. He said that he would be absent for two days. I don't know where he is, but apparently he will be here at the meeting tomorrow. Momcilo Krajisnik: Okay."

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you will see similar conversations, the next two, but it's Krajisnik inquiring about a commissioner in a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next is tab 120, master tab number 410, another intercepted phone conversation. And the English, Your Honour, begins on page 1, right after the introductory remarks. Could you tell us the date of this conversation and who the speakers are before we begin?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 22nd of June, 1992. Again, it's a conversation between Momcilo Krajisnik and Mirko Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo Krajisnik: Hello. What are you up to? Mirko Krajisnik: Many things. Listen, please. Can anyone ... Since Radovanovic is not here ... I don't know where he is. In the end of the day, he has the only copy of the document regarding the establishment of the War Commission. Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes. Mirko Krajisnik: Is there anywhere a copy of that so that someone can send it to us by fax? Hello? Momcilo Krajisnik: Yes, I can hear you. Mirko Krajisnik: Because the basic document for conduct of work is essential to make it function. Momcilo Krajisnik: So instruction should be sent to you for the Commission, is that so? Mirko Krajisnik: Can you do that? Momcilo Krajisnik: I will. Mirko Krajisnik: The decision by which ... are determined and formed -- please, 467-376. Momcilo Krajisnik: 376. Mirko Krajisnik: Yes. Momcilo Krajisnik: I will now ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, is there any -- do we know who started this telephone conversation? Who called who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it's Mirko calling Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's asking for the instructions -- he's looking for a copy of the decision on the formation of War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the initiative was on Mirko's side --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirko, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and the question also came from Mirko.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, can you send it, and Momcilo says that he will send -- fax a copy of the instruction on the War Commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next, Your Honours, is presentation tab 421, master tab 409. The excerpt begins on page 5 of the English, near the top. And at the top of page 3022-0986 in the B/C/S for Mr. Krajisnik. It's reportedly a conversation on the 26th of June between Momcilo Krajisnik and Mandic. This is a longer excerpt.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Momcilo Mandic: No, no, no ... President, what are we going to do, do send a commissioner to Kasindol, two - three men ... some Papazi, they came to me from Dr. Avramovic from Kasindol, nobody ever called, they scattered there doctor. They appoint their own people for directors. Momcilo Krajisnik: And who is that one? Momcilo Mandic: To Kasindol, the hospital. Momcilo Krajisnik: Who are those people, where is that from ... Momcilo Mandic: Local community of Kasindol, the Crisis Staff. Momcilo Krajisnik: And is that the municipality, which one? Momcilo Mandic: No, it's local community Ilidza, Ilidza is the municipality, Kasindol is local community. Momcilo Krajisnik: And why do they have the Commissioner, why don't they go there? Momcilo Mandic: No, it isn't, I don't know which ... these doctors came to me, they appointed some ... Divljan Sonja, instead of this director ... Momcilo Krajisnik: And how could they do that? Momcilo Mandic: The crisis staff of the local community Kasindol appointed her. Momcilo Krajisnik: Give me, please ... Momcilo Mandic: And than ... Popovic Koviljka, the cashier, to make an overview to see how the income is being distributed, and the income again ... Momcilo Krajisnik: I will now call Prstojevic to go there or to send someone because he has the Crisis staff Ilidza, and that is Ilidza. Momcilo Mandic: It's a disgrace, President. Momcilo Krajisnik: I will see that they take care of that immediately. Momcilo Mandic: But they are in touch with Prstojevic. Momcilo Krajisnik: See then, if he does not do anything, we'll see to send someone else there. Momcilo Mandic: They are in some kind of business with that Prstojevic, they do black-marketing together ... Momcilo Krajisnik: He cannot do anything on his own, he has the Committee now, some wonderful people are there, you know? They are not the old ones any more."

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I would note that although the English translation says committee, the word in the original is provanista [phoen] which we have been translating as commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Any other comment on that one?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly, Krajisnik is aware of who is in the War Commission in Ilidza, and that he can tell Prstojevic what to do. He will contact Prstojevic and tell him what to do, and there are good people in the commission who will make sure that this matter is taken care of. So, again, further evidence of Krajisnik's contacts with War Commissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now I want to move to another Assembly session from November of 1992, which there's a discussion about the war commissioners.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is very important for understanding or shedding light on how war commissioners worked and what --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me identify where we're at. This is presentation tab 122, master tab 411. And I believe you have several excerpts. Can you tell us, first of all, who the first speaker is --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first speaker is Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And tell the Judges where we're starting in the English.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is on page 104, the -- well, it's all one large paragraph, about one-third of the way down, the sentence starting "the commissioners." There's been a discussion in the Assembly about War Commissions and war commissioners, and Krajisnik is, in this speech, responding to earlier comments, and then there will be other speeches by other -- by some actual war commissioners following.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I inquire if Mr. Krajisnik is able to see the highlighted portion in B/C/S on his screen? Otherwise we'll read out the location for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik confirms by nodding that he has it on his screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could proceed, Ms. Hanson.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. "The commissioners are deputies whose duty are to go around the country where the government is not functioning, collect information about what is wrong, and try to help solving the problems and establishing the government. Where there is the Assembly, where there is the executive committee, it is not the parallel government nor executive government but some decree in government. In my experience, this works very well. I was informed about each one of our members who went there. Mirko Mijatovic, Jovo Mijatovic, Cancar, Marko Simic, Branko Simic, and Vojo Maksimovic have all performed that duty and solved a lot of problems." He goes on lower in the same paragraph to say that: "The purpose was to bring help in that way, and we had many municipalities asking for people to come. And it was done very efficiently. We did not cover everything, but that is a small deficiency. Therefore, we should not talk badly about this service, because it is very important to have our deputies go around talking to people. Whether he is deputy or commissioner is of no importance, but it has a great effect when a member of our Assembly comes among the people. Branko Simic has been on the Ozren mountain, Vojo Maksimovic was in Herzegovina. The people mark that as positive. Mirko Mijatovic was in Foca. And it is no parallel political organ but help for these organs to govern. And if it is not needed, we will easily abolish it." On the next page in the English translation, I just noted, again, Krajisnik's short speech, page 105 of the translation. He is responding to earlier comments about some political problems in one municipality, some conflict between some individuals. And it's notable here that he says that these comments should be investigated. He asks Branko Simic to schedule a meeting and investigate the information. I found that indicative of his -- of Krajisnik's ability as speaker of the Assembly, when he hears something that's troubling, to order an investigation. But I didn't see such a reaction to some of the -- to any of the comments I've given -- shown so far. Then there's a long speech by Vojislav Maksimovic, starting at the very bottom of page 105, but I'm looking at page 106. Vojislav Maksimovic was president of the SDS Deputy's Club, and as we know, commissioner in Herzegovina. He says -- again it's one long paragraph on page 106, but the -- about the eighth line down, he says -- seventh line down: "I was assigned in two regions in old and eastern Herzegovina." He says he had the tasks assigned by the decision "or some special instructions we received orally." He then goes on to describe how commissioners helped form authorities in the regions where the authority was still not formed, especially those regions "where we still did not have our Serbian authority, but it was formed later." He explains how commissioners get the work of executive bodies and municipal Assembly up and running and functioning. He also says in the middle of page 106: "A commissioner is also obligated to coordinate military and civilian authorities where their cooperation is not good." In the next sentence, he notes the psychological effect of having a commissioner that "some regions might not feel forgotten, and that a member of the Presidency has come there and helped with some practical issues." At the bottom of this page, he notes that "commissioners have the obligation to report what he observed to members of the Presidency." He notes the importance of the visit of Mr. Koljevic to Herzegovina, "when all the deputies, municipal presidents and commissioners met, which was of great importance." The very last line in that -- on that page: "The very territorial distance from the centre requests that we be present, that we be the people who will convey the information to the area we are responsible for." I'm now on the top of page 107. "Of course, sometimes they need to convey certain decisions as well as some informations they learn," so he's showing how the commissioners convey decisions from the Presidency and information from the municipalities back to the Presidency. At the end of that same paragraph, he says there are also many practical issues where the commissioners are always requested to help intervene, contact the government, and so on. And in his -- the next paragraph, his last paragraph of his speech, he says that "the War Presidency," in this case he's referring to the republican War Presidency, "should be the one who would decide when commissioners are needed and how many of them." So Maksimovic, as a commissioners, describes very well the work he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Before you leave Mr. Maksimovic, I wanted to ask you a question. He made reference to having received special instructions orally.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That -- I noted that as a significant indication that there's not a documentary record for all the instructions that commissioners -- he clearly was meeting with some members of the Presidency and getting instructions orally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there's no reference in the speech as to who that was?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who was the member of the Presidency assigned the responsibility for war commissioners?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you go on to your final segment in this session.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On page 109, we have the speech by Mirko Mijatovic, a deputy from Trebinje, who was assigned as commissioner for Foca. In his first paragraph on page 109 he says he was a commissioner. "They were necessary in some regions and they are still necessary." He notes the importance of the appearance of Vojislav Maksimovic, who was the previous speaker, so he confirms, as Maksimovic did, the importance of commissioners. It is a long speech. On page 110, he is talking about what's been accomplished, that Maksimovic did constitute a commission in Foca. "That is the only organ of authority --" I'm sorry, in Trebinje. Maksimovic was in Trebinje. But he, Mijatovic, was in Foca. Also did some work in Rudo and Cajnice. Most importantly, on the last page of his speech, page 111 in the translation, a third line down, he says: "If they cancel the War Commissions, I will send a report to the president who sent me." So reporting -- it says that he will be reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know which president he would have been referring to there?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He simply says "president," which tends to be the word for the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And at that time, was there a single president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to speak with any certainty about the republican level. I focused --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll ask the Judges to recall Mr. Treanor's testimony on that point.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me then go to another topic. We've finished talking about war commissioners for a while. In your report, at paragraph 45, you discuss the military role of Crisis Staffs, and I think this will take us back to a question Judge Hanoteau asked us earlier.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want to give us a little introductory remark about that before we look at the first document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I may have made my comments already, but that it's a very -- of all the issues dealing with Crisis Staffs, of all the areas of responsibility of the Crisis Staffs, the question of the military role has the most variations. As I said, there's a range of responsibility and authority -- responsibility for an authority over the military claimed by Crisis Staffs for a number of reasons. Some have to do with simply who -- what were the military structures already in place. Was there a JNA unit? Who was in command of that unit? And, also as we'll see, the personality of the Crisis Staff or other people -- municipal leaders. Another important factor is -- and perhaps the most important factor of all, is the question of time, because, as we saw before, Crisis Staffs themselves were bodies in transition, moving from secret party organs to public municipal authorities, and the military structures in question were also in transition at this time. So whenever we talk about how much authority a particular Crisis Staff had or claimed to have over military units, we have to think about what was the state of the military structures at the time. Because when Crisis Staffs were first formed, as we saw, in December 1992, there was, of course, the JNA. The Yugoslav People's Army was present in Bosnia, stationed in various parts of the country. There was also the republican Territorial Defence, which had its own republican chain of command. With the withdrawal of the JNA, the VRS, the army of the Bosnian Serb Republic, was established, but it took, of course, some time for those structures to be up and running. And Crisis Staffs basically filled a gap between a JNA that was withdrawing or disintegrating or not following the orders of its own command structure and the then VRS as it was being established. So we have to remember that the military structures were in transition. We have to look at the time period to understand this very complicated issue. What we do see everywhere, however -- the common factor is the coordination of defence. Crisis Staffs had a role to communicate with the military, to support them. Sometimes that role included giving, as we saw, recommendations or even orders to certain units. But of all the issues, as I said, this is the least amenable to one pattern. But there is definitely a consistent trend. I think looking at the practical examples will make it much clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then with that, Your Honours, the next tab will be tab 123. However, before we put that up, that's a copy of the instructions --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I simply -- I wanted to point out what the normative document says about the role of Crisis Staffs - we looked at them only yesterday so perhaps we need not spend much time - but that they always mention a military role for the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in the variant A and variant B document, generally, what was the role of the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, remember that one of the -- the primary purpose of the instructions was to enhance the mobility and readiness for defence of the interests of the Serbian people. We know that they were to include the commander of the TO in the Crisis Staff; they were to mobilise the TO and police reserves; they were also to subordinate those police to the commands of the JNA. So there was definitely a military role, but the JNA was seen as the body with whom to coordinate and, indeed, subordinate. And that was -- remember, these were written in December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: December?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of 1991, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That was tab 123, master tab 22. The next tab in the presentation binder is 124, master tab 76. Again, this is a document we've seen before, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Djeric's instructions for the operation of Crisis Staffs from 26 April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And these specifically addressed some of the issues regarding the relationship between Crisis Staffs and military units, no?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once again, we see that -- excuse me. Under Article 4, it notes that: "Command over the Territorial Defence and the police force is exclusively the responsibility of the professional staff. It is, therefore, necessary to prevent any interference as to the commanding of the Territorial Defence or the use of the police force." We see an acknowledgement that command of the forces is a matter for professional staff, but recall, again, that the commander of the TO and the police were members of the Crisis Staff, so they -- the Crisis Staff was to make sure that no outside influence, is how I take this, is to interfere in the professional staff commanding. Under number 8, the Crisis Staff is to create normal life and work conditions of the JNA, to ensure proper relations and generally to enable the JNA to work. Again, this was 26 April, 1992. The JNA was still the official arm -- army of the -- of Yugoslavia. It was still present in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab number 25 in the presentation binder, master tab 108.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, these are all documents we've seen before. Simply to revisit the military question. These are Plavsic's instructions of the 24th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When it was proposed to create War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: War Presidencies. But, again, the first task, under item 1, the first task of these Presidencies is the organisation, coordination and synchronisation of the activities for the defence of the Serbian people, so clearly a role in organising military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And tab --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: And furthermore -- I'm sorry, I don't have the -- okay, thank you. Yes. Furthermore, the commissioner, who, as we know, is to be appointed to these War Presidencies -- to these Presidencies, was "to ensure the constant coordination and implementation of the policies and measures determined and issued by republic state organs and the Main Staff of this Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." By this date, the 24th of May, the VRS had been formally established, although not yet up and running. But we see the transition now. Instead of working with the JNA, they are to coordinate the implementation of the policies of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move to presentation tab 126, and master tab 110. Again, another document that we've seen before. Does this also speak to the issue of Crisis Staffs and military units?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As we've seen before, it's very similar wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what is this document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, this is the Presidency decision of 31 May 1992 on the formation of War Presidencies in municipalities. And the wording for the relevant sections is almost the same as Plavsic's instructions: "Coordination of defence and implementation of the policies of the General Staff," or -- yes, the Main Staff, I'm sorry, of the army of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then following close on that, tab 127, master tab 112, which is a June 10th decision regarding War Commissions. What did that say about the topic?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under Article 4 -- I'm sorry, Article 3. Under Article 3: "War Commissions shall cooperate with the authorities with a view to creating conditions for the work of military organs and units engaged in defending the Serbian people." As I said before, the War Commissions -- the emphasis in this decision is on getting to normality, getting all the regular state organs up and running. So we see in this decision a slightly different emphasis, that the War Commission is to create the conditions for the military organs to work, just as it is also supposed to create the conditions for the municipal Assembly and other municipal organs to work. This was, of course, dated 10 June 1992, and it's an indication that there is more military command structure being established, and military organs. But nonetheless, it remains close coordination and support at the municipal level for those developing military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I have two tabs to finish this binder. It may take me a minute or two past 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab 128, Ms. Hanson, master tab 100, I believe, is a document that we may have talked about before from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We saw -- this is the decision on the organisation and work of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor municipality. We've seen it before in connection with the instructions -- Djeric's instructions of April 1992. And in echoing Djeric's instructions, it indicates the role of the Crisis Staff in organising and coordinating measures of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you address particularly Articles 2, 6, and 9.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. Article 2, it shows that the Crisis Staff is being established to defend municipal territory, provide security for the population. So in addition to other municipal, governmental functions, there is a function of defence and security. And Article 6 is the most clear on its defence functions. "The Crisis Staff shall coordinate the work and activities of all protagonists in the system of all people's defence; review questions related to mobilisation, the development and reinforcement of the armed forces and other structures, fostering cooperation between these structures and the competent municipal authorities; resolve questions related to the material and financial requirements of the TO on the basis of special requests made by the commander of the Municipal TO Staff; keep abreast of the situation in the municipality and all vital aspects of the armed struggle and shall, accordingly, undertake the necessary measures; monitor recruiting activities and intervene when necessary to ensure they are implemented." Article 9: "The Crisis Staff shall maintain constant cooperation with units of the JNA, the Territorial Defence, Civilian Protection, and the public security system via the senior officers of these institutions and organs and, through the municipality's executive committee, with all other economic and social subjects in the municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the last one before the break, if we could go to tab 129, master tab 72. This is an excerpt from the March 27th Assembly session. And I believe the English, on page 10 at the bottom, the speaker is shown as Dr. Radovan Karadzic. The highlighted portion you wanted to talk about is on the following page. I have a copy here for the usher.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's page 19 and 20, I think, not 10. It's on page 20 in the translation. Again, we've seen this speech of Karadzic before, but since I'm talking about the question of the military authorities and the military structures, I look at it again in a new light. He says: "When you return to your municipalities, form Crisis Staffs. Find a number of reserve officers for those staffs and have them register everyone who owns weapons as well as units. They should organise Territorial Defence. And if the JNA is there, they must be placed under its command; if not, let them be placed under the command of reserve officers." Again, one factor, this is the geographical factor, is there a JNA unit there. The last two paragraphs on page 20: "If war breaks out, you will get the plans, but I urge you to immediately organise the people within Territorial Defence units headed by reserve officers. Form squads, platoons, and Crisis Staffs and engage retired officers. This must be done throughout our areas."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I appreciate the extra time to finish that binder. We'll have a new presentation binder passed up before we start the next session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we adjourn, the copies that have now been distributed, the binders, is there one for Mr. Krajisnik as well, or --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm still waiting for some answers in respect of the issue raised by Mr. Stewart. It might be wiser not to try to deal with the matter with incomplete information during this break. But if the parties would be available, even after this hearing, to see whether we can resolve the matter. Then we'll adjourn until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, before I give you the opportunity to proceed, are we more or less on schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think we are. I had anticipated it would take all of the rest of the week for me to finish with Ms. Hanson, that I would finish by the end of the day Friday. I actually told Mr. Stewart earlier, I think I will finish sometime around the end of the first session or before the second session on Friday. My estimate may change as we move slower and faster, but right now I think we're on schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it might be -- if I could, because it will only take a couple of seconds -- well, that's not literal. But I mentioned to Mr. Hannis -- I wasn't going to mention it right now, but it's convenient as it follows on from that. On Mr. Hannis's projected schedule, Your Honour, the timetable then has allowed Monday and Tuesday for this witness, and I would expect to be able to complete the cross-examination of this witness on Monday and Tuesday, and then there's another witness coming on Wednesday. Your Honour, taking my chances entirely as to when exactly Mr. Hannis finishes on Friday, it would be terribly helpful, Your Honour, if we were then -- if Your Honours were then willing to stop and allow me that extra time to spend with Mr. Krajisnik on Friday, in other words, not start cross-examination then but then break -- we don't know whether it's going to be an hour or an hour and a half or something like that. But then I would cross-examine on Monday and Tuesday and Your Honour would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider it, let's say it this way at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Your Honour has the point. It is very difficult to get ample time with Mr. Krajisnik. Can I just say, for example, that Ms. Loukas has to see tomorrow in relation with other witnesses. I'm sure Your Honours are well aware of the tightness and the pressures to get that time. And if we go to a quarter to 2.00, it's 3.00 by the time we start, and Your Honour knows how little time, in practice, is available one once gets through security in order to spend time with one's client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of it. Mr. Hannis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think we have the new binders, number 4, for you on the registrar's desk. And we'll hand one copy to Ms. Hanson, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first tab in that binder is presentation tab 130, which is master tab number 40. Ms. Hanson, I think this is a document as part of your discussion about cooperation between the Crisis Staffs and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a document we've seen before. The conclusions of the municipal board of the SDS Zvornik of the 22nd of December forming the Crisis Staff. In this context, I would note at the bottom, the list of the members of the Crisis Staff, that the command staff of the Zvornik municipality JNA is listed as a member, indicating that the general intent of the 19 December instructions of cooperation and coordination with the command staff of the JNA is being followed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next tab, tab 131 in the presentation, master tab 260.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is minutes of a meeting of the Crisis Staff held on the 29th of January, 1992, it says, in the local community of Lukavica, but it appears to be the Novo Sarajevo Crisis Staffs. But it's not -- I just say that on the basis of the membership that we saw in earlier decisions. But it just --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it indicates Lukavica as the location --

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Location, yes. Here, under number 10, on the second page in the original but number 10 on the first page of the translation: "All battalion commanders are to be called to the Crisis Staff meeting. In charge of this is Momo Garic." You'll recall that Momo Garic was one of the speakers in an intercepted phone conversation with Momcilo Krajisnik that we listened to before the break. So once again, the invitation to battalion commanders indicates the coordination, exchange of information, with -- between Crisis Staffs and military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next is presentation tab 132, master tab 259.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness raise the microphones a little bit, thank you, so that we avoid the noise of paper-shuffling. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I believe this is an interview with a military officer, and you want to talk about particular excerpts?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is an interview from May of 1994 in a daily newspaper of VRS with Colonel Zelja, who was then the commander of the 43rd Prijedor Brigade. In April 1992, as he explains in this - excuse me - interview, he was deputy commander. He is describing the cooperation between the JNA and the SDS leadership in Prijedor. On page -- it's a little difficult to follow the original because it's a newspaper article in columns, so to say exactly where it is -- I have the right one up on the Sanction right now. But on page 3 -- that was good. Page 3 in the translation -- I just want to see -- yes. They're talking about the time when the brigade came to Prijedor after fighting in Slavonia, so this is the winter of 1991/1992. And Zelja says: "The brigade commander was immediately linked to the leadership of the SDS, giving them important support, as they do for all decent Serbs, to organise themselves for self-defence in case of an attack by the Muslim forces". At the bottom of this same speech of his, he says: "We have never given up these goals, and it is the creation of a Serbian state in these areas." So he says, as soon as the command arrived, they were linked with the leadership of the SDS. On page 4 in the translation, in the middle of page -- well, the second paragraph of his speech, he says: "We then offered maximal help and support to the SDS, both in organising preparations and in advising them, in order to overcome certain problems and to take power. Such cooperation was also established with the leaders of the party, the people in power, the Crisis Staff, and all decent Serbs who were, and still are, are of importance for this town." That's what I had highlighted from that section, indicating the way that certain people in the JNA command did cooperate with the -- make contact with the SDS and did help the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. If we could go next to presentation tab 133, and it is master tab number 261. Can you tell us what that document is and what it shows?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order from - well, it's described as minutes on the second page - from Colonel General Blagoje Adzic, the Federal Secretary of National Defence of the FRY, that is, of the JNA, of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It's a bit confusing because the first page is a cover sheet. What he's -- the interesting page is on -- yes, on page 2, the Federal Secretary gave the tasking: "In the shortest possible time, form the staffs, squads, and brigades of voluntary units of the reduced structure and adequately re-enforce them with the JNA officers, weaponry and equipment, the voluntary units to be militarily organised and connected to the JNA commands in their area of responsibility." This is in regard specifically to Bosnia. Although it doesn't say what kind of voluntary units, as we'll see in practice, this is consistent with the forming of voluntary units of the SDS and their cooperation with JNA commands. So the fact that this was a tasking by the federal secretary of defence shows that the kind of contacts and cooperation Zelja was talking about as individual actions were becoming more and more army policy, or at least open -- openly acknowledged in the JNA, as we see in the next document, more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which is tab 134 in the presentation binder, and master tab number 263. Can you tell us who this is from and whom it's to?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a regular operative report of the reserve command post of the 2nd Military District to the command of the 2nd Military District Operations Centre, dated the 6th of April, 1992. And in the middle of the page, it says-- he reports: "We have remained in constant contact and coordination of operations with the Pale Crisis Staff." So a JNA unit is reporting constant contact and coordination with a Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next, we have another one which, I think you'd indicated, shows a little different perspective. This is tab number 135 in the presentation, master tab 276, from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the minutes of a meeting of the municipal board of SDS Prijedor, on the 23rd of April, 1992. You will recall that this is shortly before the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and, therefore, the army of Yugoslavia was declared, so the future of the JNA was still unclear at this point. And we see the decisions of the municipal board. Number 1, "to approach the garrison command and ask them if they were going to protect the Serbs in the event of a conflict or not." Then under number 5, "to immediately start working on the takeover, the coordination with the JNA notwithstanding." Under 6, "Put the point across. If Zelja JNA does not declare that the JNA is indeed going to protect the Serbs, the SDS will call upon all Serbian soldiers to leave the JNA and take all their weapons." This is the same Zelja that we saw the interview with, who, in retrospective, is saying what good contacts we had. But we can see that they're still not entirely sure to what extent the JNA is going to back their plans, but they plan to go ahead regardless of the stance of the JNA. As we saw from the interview, however, the JNA does, in fact, back their plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, let me move to a related topic. Moving from the JNA, were there other types of military units that were involved with the Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is what further complicates the picture, because in addition to the federal army of the JNA, each republic also had its own Territorial Defence, which was organised and managed at the municipal level, with its own republic command structure reaching to the republican level. So one issue was, as we saw, is there a JNA command in the area, and to what extent they will cooperate with the Crisis Staffs, and the Crisis Staffs with them. Another issue is then the local Territorial Defence forces. And, in those places, the influence of the Crisis Staffs over the Territorial Defence depended, in part, on how much control the SDS and Crisis Staff over municipal organs, including the municipal TO staff. But until the formation of the VRS, the Serb TO was essentially the military force of the Serb Republic, because of the transition of the JNA. So another aspect is the relations with the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let's talk about presentation tab 136, master tab number 241, in that regard.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This also indicates that, in some places, the Crisis Staffs, or the SDS in general, where they might not control the Territorial Defence, also formed its own units; sometimes secretly, sometimes fairly openly, calling them Serb Territorial Defences. Again, the openness or the secrecy depended on a number of factors, especially their control over the municipality. But here we see in Sanski Most, because these are the conclusions of a meeting of the Crisis Staff, held on 21 and 22 April 1992, of Sanski Most, under item 6: "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most hereby adopts the conclusion that the Serbian defence forces are to be placed at the disposal of the commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence and engaged as a special unit of the Serbian Territorial Defence." And here we have the formation of a Serb Territorial Defence based on, in this case, a unit calling it -- a force called the Serbian defence forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you about the situation in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tab number 137 in the presentation is master tab 221. And the title page of this refers to it as a report on the work of the municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The internal evidence in the -- of this report indicates it's a report summarising the work of the municipal Assembly and War Presidency from the 1st of January, 1992, to 20 April 1993. So it's giving a retrospective on the work of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you direct the Court to the excerpts that you're going to talk about, and the page number?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 4 of the English translation, which is -- if I could see the whole of the B/C/S, it is 0552816. That's for the first section --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The ERN is rather hard to read on the Sanction presentation, but it looks like it's page number 2 at the top?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Last paragraph, page 2 at the top of the B/C/S. First full paragraph on page 4 of the English translation. This report is noting that "SDS members in the Serbian police reserve, the Serbian municipality and TO staff, and the municipal SDS subcommittee for defence and protection of the Serbian people stepped up their efforts to prepare the Serbian people for war." At the bottom of this same paragraph, it talks about that individuals were -- who were involved. "This is a report on their work, and the protagonists were Serbs, members of the SDS. So here we will mention just a few of them, those who are the most responsible, and they are: Miroslav Vjestica, Dmitar Ziganovic, Drago Damjanic, Mile Vojinovic, Mile Mijic, Drago Skoric, and others who worked in parallel in providing weapons and organising reserve units of the Serbian police and units of the Serbian Territorial Defence, as well as those who worked to organise and establish government authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask to stop, because I sought the assistance of the registrar. But my tab 137 is empty so I can't make any notes on it. If you will just allow me 30 seconds to re-find in the transcript what I missed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to assure Your Honour that there's no conspiracy on our part to deprive you of the documents. I know that's the second time it's happened, and it appears you're the only victim so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Conspiracy is a typical, I would say, English/American concept of law, so I'm unfamiliar with it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Hanson, if you could continue.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've finished that section. I'm just trying to identify the next section. In this same document, on page 6 of the English translation -- I'm trying to find it in the B/C/S, it's on page number -- seen as page 4 in the B/C/S. The ERN ends in 18. It's the first paragraph -- first full paragraph on page 6 in the English translation. "Another task which had to be handled by part of the War Presidency was the integration of Serbian Territorial Defence units into the 10th Corps of the JNA to avoid the situation in which we would be declared and treated as paramilitaries." So we see that the SDS and Crisis Staff members were involved in forming certain Territorial Defence units. They were then integrated into the JNA corps. If you can recall Adzic's order on staffing JNA -- of volunteer units and putting them under JNA command, this is consistent with that tasking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Is there anything else in that document?

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: We'll come to it later in another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I want to now go to an Assembly session excerpt. This is the 1995 Assembly. And I'd ask you if we have Mr. Karadzic talking about the formation of SDS units during this time.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Karadzic's speech, as you said, in April 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Let me note the tab number. Presentation tab 138, master tab 49. And if you could tell the Judges where you're beginning.

utterances.speaker: DOROTHEA HANSON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm beginning on page 323 of the English, going on to 324. We've seen this speech earlier as his recollection of the A and B document, but I would like to give a slightly longer excerpt because he also discusses the military preparations. In the middle of the lower paragraph on page 323, he talks about how, "when the war began, we had municipal power, we held it firmly." He reminds the Assemblymen of the A and B variant document. He says: "In the B variant, where we were in the minority, 20 per cent/15 per cent, we had set up a government and a brigade, a unit no matter what size, but there was a detachment with a commander." Then at the last two lines of that paragraph -- of that page: "Distribution of weapons was carried out thanks to the JNA. What could be withdrawn was withdrawn and distributed to the people in the Serbian areas." We're now at the top of page 324. "But it was the SDS which organised the people and created the army. It was an army. Together with the police, those were the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They created the space, liberated and created the space. In some places, with the help of the JNA; in others, without the help of the JNA; and in yet others, without the JNA knowledge, since Huso and Juso were commanding in the JNA at that time. And what happened? We made various calculations and agreements with Yugoslavia. We decided to set up the TO, the Serbian brigades, which were indeed led by the SDS, but not as a party army but as a people's army." And finally in this same speech, seven lines up from the bottom of page 324, he says: "The corps of the army existed in every municipality. I would like to hear in which municipality it does not exist." I think this is the best summary of how they formed units and, in some places, had the help of the JNA; in other places, they hid it from the JNA, because, when there's reference to Huso and Juso - I believe just a generic Muslim name - in some places, Muslims were commanding in the JNA and they hid from them the formation of units led by the SDS. And, of course, in connection -- he refers to the 19 December instructions at the beginning of this passage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
